# **Quantifying Lodging Occupancy for Building Energy Performance: An Analytical Evidence Base for Canadian Hotel Energy Modeling**

Evaluating the energy consumption of lodging buildings requires a highly granular and defensible evidence base for occupant presence. Traditional datasets, such as national time-use surveys, systematically omit hotel guests because residents are rarely sampled as guests within their own municipalities, and international tourists remain entirely out of frame. Consequently, building energy modelers must synthesize commercial hospitality metrics, national tourism indicators, and building energy code standards to construct realistic representation schedules. This report establishes a comprehensive framework for compiling authoritative lodging data, defining diurnal occupant schedules, tracking historical trajectories, and forecasting monthly occupancy to the year 2030, culminating in a robust mathematical formulation to couple monthly and diurnal schedules.

## **Directory of Authoritative Hotel Occupancy Data Sources in Canada**

To establish a defensible baseline for building energy models, several public, commercial, and open-source datasets must be integrated. These sources vary in coverage, geographic resolution, and update frequency. The primary commercial authority is STR, a subsidiary of CoStar Group, which aggregates physical occupancy, Average Daily Rate (ADR), and Revenue Per Available Room (RevPAR) from a vast global sample of lodging properties.1 For public-sector context, Statistics Canada publishes several annual and monthly series tracking financial performance, business status, and international arrivals.2 Additionally, provincial tourism boards and local open-data platforms provide regional data that are highly valuable for localized building simulations.4

The structural differences between these data sources are crucial. While Statistics Canada Table 33-10-0102-01 provides high-fidelity financial insights, it does not publish monthly physical occupancy rates.2 Instead, public agencies and academic modelers rely on the Tourism Data Collective or STR licensing to acquire physical occupancy rates.3 Commercial data from STR capture submarket nuances, which is essential because airport hotels, suburban motels, and downtown luxury towers exhibit vastly different occupancy amplitudes and seasonal profiles.10

## **Diurnal Guest-Presence Profiles and Building Energy Model Schedules**

Within a hotel guest room, occupant presence dictates internal sensible and latent heat gains, domestic hot water demand, lighting usage, and plug loads.14 These elements directly influence the dynamic thermal loads of the building envelope, requiring precise schedule definitions. Prior to the post-pandemic stabilization, research indicated that hotel guest rooms remained unoccupied for approximately 70% of the day, yet accounted for up to 80% of total building energy consumption.14 This underscores the importance of capturing the thermal transition between occupied and vacant states.  
In professional building energy simulation, standardized baseline models are defined by the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings (NECB) and the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) Standard 90.1 prototype building specifications.16 The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) maintains the Large Hotel Prototype, which serves as the foundational reference model.18 This prototype represents a 122,132 square foot, six-story structure with a conditioned basement, housing a total of 179 guest rooms that constitute approximately 41% of the total floor area.18  
The diurnal guest-presence profile differs significantly between weekdays and weekends. During weekdays, occupancy typically peaks overnight, experiences a rapid decline during the morning hours as business travelers depart, remains at a low baseline throughout the day, and rises steadily in the evening.19 On weekends, the daytime drop-off is less pronounced, reflecting the staggered schedules of leisure travelers, who return to their rooms earlier or remain in them longer during the morning.19

| Hour of Day | Weekday Occupancy Fraction | Weekend Occupancy Fraction | Weekday Lighting Fraction | Weekend Lighting Fraction | Weekday Receptacle Fraction | Weekend Receptacle Fraction |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **01:00 \- 06:00** | 0.90 \- 0.95 | 0.95 | 0.10 \- 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| **06:00 \- 08:00** | 0.80 \- 0.60 | 0.90 \- 0.80 | 0.40 \- 0.60 | 0.30 \- 0.50 | 0.50 \- 0.70 | 0.40 \- 0.60 |
| **08:00 \- 12:00** | 0.40 \- 0.20 | 0.60 \- 0.40 | 0.30 \- 0.15 | 0.40 \- 0.25 | 0.40 \- 0.25 | 0.40 \- 0.30 |
| **12:00 \- 17:00** | 0.15 \- 0.20 | 0.30 \- 0.35 | 0.15 | 0.20 | 0.25 | 0.30 |
| **17:00 \- 19:00** | 0.40 \- 0.60 | 0.55 \- 0.70 | 0.50 \- 0.70 | 0.60 \- 0.80 | 0.50 \- 0.65 | 0.55 \- 0.75 |
| **19:00 \- 22:00** | 0.75 \- 0.85 | 0.80 \- 0.90 | 0.80 \- 0.90 | 0.85 \- 0.95 | 0.70 \- 0.85 | 0.75 \- 0.90 |
| **22:00 \- 24:00** | 0.90 | 0.90 \- 0.95 | 0.40 \- 0.20 | 0.50 \- 0.30 | 0.40 \- 0.30 | 0.45 \- 0.35 |

The simulation of these lodging profiles requires different schedules for guest rooms, public lobbies, corridors, and back-of-house areas.18 In the ASHRAE / PNNL Large Hotel Prototype, the thermal zones are partitioned to isolate these distinct functional spaces 18:

* **Guest Rooms:** Run on the highly variable diurnal schedules detailed above. In modern simulations, to model the energy savings associated with occupancy sensors, these continuous fractional curves are often discretized into zone-by-zone binary state schedules (0 or 1\) representing localized guest presence.18  
* **Lobby / Reception:** Modeled using a continuous, near-24-hour occupancy schedule that peaks during check-in windows (typically 3:00 PM to 7:00 PM) and maintains a baseline level of staff and traveler activity overnight.20  
* **Back-of-House / Laundry / Kitchens:** Scheduled to align with operations. Laundry rooms are scheduled around morning housekeeping cycles, whereas industrial kitchens and banquet halls on upper floors run on intensive, highly episodic schedules tied to meal times.18  
* **Corridors:** Typically modeled with low, constant occupancy fractions but continuous lighting schedules, except where occupancy-sensor-driven dimming controls are applied.

Under the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings (NECB) guidelines, the performance path compares the proposed design's energy budget against a reference baseline.22 The NECB mandates specific rules for guest rooms that differ from commercial zones. For instance, the NECB requires occupancy sensor controls in guest rooms designed to automatically turn off lighting within 20 minutes of vacancy.23 Furthermore, guest rooms are the only spaces within the NECB framework that mandate automatic receptacle control to mitigate standby plug loads.23 To capture these mandatory interventions, energy modelers must adjust baseline lighting and receptacle fractional runtimes downward when occupancy sensors are implemented, preventing the overestimation of base energy consumption.24

## **Monthly Seasonality and the COVID-19 Trajectory in Canadian Hospitality**

Canadian hospitality is subject to strong monthly and seasonal variations driven by geography and climate.26 The national lodging market exhibits a highly pronounced summer peak, centered in July and August, when international arrivals and domestic leisure travel reach their maximum.1 Conversely, deep winter troughs occur in January and February, when travel is dominated by business trips and localized ski tourism.27  
This seasonal equilibrium was severely disrupted by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020\. The subsequent years were characterized by a sharp collapse, a highly volatile domestic recovery, an inflationary revenue surge, and eventually a transition toward stabilized, single-digit growth.

 ──\> \[2020 Collapse\] ──\> ──\> ──\>

| Year | National Lodging Revenue | Hotel Subsector Margin | Physical Occupancy Trend | Key Market Drivers & Context |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **2019** | $26.9 Billion (Subsector) 6 | 14.2% 6 | \~65% Peak Baseline | Pre-pandemic baseline with balanced international, business, and leisure segments.2 |
| **2020** | Severe Contraction | \~4.6% 21 | \< 30% (Urban Troughs \< 15%) 29 | Structural collapse due to international travel bans, domestic quarantine mandates, and lockdowns.29 |
| **2021** | $19.5 Billion 21 | 11.5% 21 | August Peak: 65.6% 26 | Highly domestic, self-contained travel. Nature-oriented and rural accommodations (cabins, campgrounds) significantly outperformed urban commercial hotels.21 |
| **2022** | $29.6 Billion 2 | 17.5% 2 | Gradual Recovery | Revenue surpassed 2019 levels by 9.6% due to 29.3% inflation in accommodation prices. International guest share remained suppressed at 14.6%.2 |
| **2023** | $34.9 Billion 6 | 18.5% 6 | Near Pre-Pandemic Baseline | Profit margins peaked at 20.0% for hotels, driven by labor shortages, wage adjustments, and the closure of less profitable properties.6 |
| **2024** | $35.9 Billion 7 | 18.0% 7 | Annual Average: 65.7% 11 | Return to normalcy. RevPAR reached a record CAD 137.17 (+28% vs. 2019). International arrivals recovered to 96% of pre-pandemic levels.11 |
| **2025** | Continued Steady Growth | \~18.0% | July Peak: 77.6% 1 | Revenue per available room (RevPAR) exceeded CAD 200 for the first time in August.31 |
| **2026** | Stabilized baseline 3 | \~18.0% | YTD (Jan-Apr): 58.3% 3 | Complete alignment with 2019 physical occupancy baselines, driven by domestic spending resilience.3 |

The recovery path reveals a deep divergence between financial performance and physical occupancy. Although total accommodation revenue surpassed 2019 levels as early as 2022, physical occupancy did not fully recover until 2024\.2 The rapid revenue recovery was a product of unprecedented price increases, with a 29.3% increase in lodging rates from 2021 to 2022\.2 Additionally, the pandemic induced a permanent structural consolidation: many independent, less resilient hotels closed, leaving a higher concentration of profitable, high-yield corporate and affiliated properties in operation.7 In 2026, the market has settled into a normalized state, characterized by single-digit revenue growth and physical occupancy rates that closely mirror the pre-pandemic 2019 benchmark.3

## **Advanced Hotel Occupancy Forecasting Methodologies to 2030**

To project monthly hotel occupancy rates to the year 2030, analysts must employ time-series forecasting models that can accommodate seasonal variation and structural shocks. Traditional univariate statistical methods are highly effective but present clear limitations when applied to datasets containing the massive volatility of the pandemic era.

### **Review of Candidate Forecasting Models**

* **Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA):** This model represents a standard for univariate time-series forecasting.33 It combines autoregressive ![][image1] and moving average ![][image2] components with non-seasonal differencing ![][image3], while capturing annual seasonal patterns through corresponding seasonal terms ![][image4], where ![][image5] for monthly series.33 SARIMA excels at projecting stable, linear seasonal structures but struggles with sudden structural breaks, often overreacting to outliers unless heavily parameterized.  
* **Error, Trend, Seasonal (ETS) State-Space Models:** The ETS framework utilizes exponential smoothing to model level, trend, and seasonal states in either additive or multiplicative forms.35 For lodging data, multiplicative seasonality is often preferred because seasonal amplitudes scale proportionally with the overall market volume.36 ETS models are highly interpretable and computationally efficient, but they assume that the underlying states evolve smoothly, making them highly susceptible to trend distortion when trained on highly volatile periods.37  
* **Structural Time-Series Models (STSM):** Also known as Unobserved Components Models (UCM), STSMs decompose a series directly into unobserved components such as the trend, cycle, and seasonal parts:  
  ![][image6]  
  This formulation allows for the direct integration of intervention analysis.34 Structural models are robust for policy and crisis evaluations because shocks can be isolated to a single component without corrupting the long-term seasonal states.34

### **The Danger of Training Models on Untreated Raw Data**

The primary pitfall in forecasting hotel occupancy to 2030 is training traditional models directly on raw monthly series that include the 2020–2022 data without adjustment. Standard estimation procedures, such as maximum likelihood, seek to minimize overall residual variance.37 If the catastrophic drop of 2020 is treated as a standard deviation, it leads to severe parameter distortion.37 This distortion manifests as:

* **Overestimated Variance:** Inflates prediction intervals, rendering the 2030 forecast bands so wide they lose practical utility for energy project planning.  
* **Seasonal Distortion:** Traditional models may interpret the sudden drop as a change in seasonal behavior, corrupting the estimated monthly seasonal factors.29  
* **Downward Trend Bias:** The historical slope is pulled downward, causing the model to project artificial market contractions or delayed recoveries up to 2030\.37

### **Recommended Forecasting Recipe**

An optimal forecasting workflow must isolate the pandemic shock to preserve the integrity of the seasonal and trend components. The analyst should execute a structural time-series intervention approach using the following sequential steps:

1. **Intervention Parameterization:** Introduce a deterministic intervention variable, ![][image7], into the time-series model.33 This is structured as a combination of a step function (capturing the sudden lockdown impact in March 2020\) and a decaying transient shock (capturing the gradual recovery phase back to baseline) 34:  
   ![][image8]  
   where ![][image9] is a step indicator, ![][image10] is a pulse indicator, and ![][image11] is a decay parameter representing the rate of market recovery.34  
2. **De-Noising and Decomposition:** Apply a robust seasonal-trend decomposition (such as STL) to isolate and temporarily extract the distorted seasonal components of the crisis years, replacing the outliers with interpolated values derived from pre-pandemic baselines.33  
3. **Exogenous Proxy Integration:** Implement a Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX) or a Mixed Data Sampling (MIDAS) model.38 Incorporate high-frequency exogenous series, such as monthly airport passenger traffic and regional search volume indices (e.g., Google Trends for travel keywords).28 These predictors act as real-time sentiment proxies, stabilizing the model during volatile periods.41  
4. **Validation via Rolling-Origin Evaluation:** Evaluate model candidates using a rolling-origin framework (expanding or windowed training sets) across one-month and three-month horizons.41 Select the model that minimizes the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) on post-recovery validation sets (2023–2026).34  
5. **Logistic Capping:** Hotel occupancy is physically bounded by zero and 100%. To prevent unconstrained linear projections from exceeding maximum physical capacities during summer peaks, apply a logistic transformation or a capped regression curve to the final forecast output.28

## **Mathematical Formulation for High-Resolution Schedule Coupling**

Once a monthly forecasted occupancy rate is obtained for the years leading to 2030, building energy modelers face the challenge of translating this monthly amplitude into a continuous, high-resolution (e.g., 30-minute) schedule. Simple multiplicative scaling can introduce thermodynamic errors. To address this, modelers can apply a spatial allocation approach to preserve localized heat gain dynamics.  
Let ![][image12] represent the 30-minute interval of a day, ![][image13] represent the day type (where ![][image14] is a standard weekday and ![][image15] is a weekend), and ![][image16] represent the calendar month.  
Let ![][image17] represent the fixed, unit-normalized diurnal occupancy profile for interval ![][image18] on day type ![][image19], defined such that:  
![][image20]  
Let ![][image21] represent the forecasted monthly average physical occupancy rate for month ![][image22] (expressed as a fraction between ![][image23] and ![][image24]).

### **Multiplicative Coupling (Aggregated Building-Level Model)**

In a simplified, single-zone, or aggregated building-level model where all guest rooms are lumped into a single thermal zone, the dynamic occupancy fraction ![][image25] is calculated as the direct product of the diurnal baseline and the monthly forecast:  
![][image26]

#### **Thermodynamic Pitfall**

This multiplicative approach is standard in building energy modeling but introduces a significant physical contradiction. If the forecasted monthly occupancy is ![][image27], the maximum peak occupancy simulated in any room overnight is scaled down to 50% of its design capacity.18 In physical reality, a hotel at 50% occupancy does not have half an occupant in every room; rather, 50% of the rooms are fully occupied (with 100% of their localized sensible and latent heat gains active), while the remaining 50% of the rooms are entirely vacant.18  
Scaling down the occupancy curve mathematically "liquefies" the occupants, distributing them evenly across all zones. This underrepresents localized thermal spikes, which can prevent simulated thermostatic controls from triggering and suppress the peak cooling loads required to size HVAC equipment accurately. Furthermore, it distorts ventilation dynamics in systems utilizing demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) based on carbon dioxide sensors, which expect binary occupant thresholds rather than a continuous, diluted baseline.43

### **Spatial Allocation and Probabilistic Coupling (Granular Space-by-Space Model)**

To maintain physical and thermodynamic accuracy in a granular multi-room simulation, the monthly average occupancy rate must be translated into a discrete number of fully occupied and vacant rooms.18  
Let ![][image28] be the total number of guest-room thermal zones in the energy model, and let ![][image29] represent the unique index of each guest room zone.18  
For any month ![][image22], the target number of occupied rooms ![][image30] is calculated by rounding the product of the total room inventory and the monthly occupancy rate:  
![][image31]  
The set of all guest-room zones is partitioned into two distinct subsets: the occupied subset ![][image32] and the vacant subset ![][image33], such that:  
![][image34]  
To prevent systematic bias (such as simulating the same rooms as occupied every month), the subset ![][image32] should be randomly selected or rotated dynamically to reflect real-world hotel guest placement strategies.43  
The occupancy schedule for room ![][image35] during month ![][image22] is then defined as:  
![][image36]  
For vacant rooms (![][image37]), the energy modeler must also adjust corresponding zone-level systems 18:

* **Lighting and Receptacles:** Set to their minimum standby fractions to capture parasitic standby loads (e.g., clock radios, smart TV standby power, and automation hubs) 14:  
  ![][image38]  
  \* **HVAC Thermostat Setpoints:** Vacant zones are placed in a setback or deadband state, allowing the room temperature to float between wider limits (e.g., ![][image39] for heating and ![][image40] for cooling) to capture the significant energy savings associated with modern guest-room energy management systems (EMS) 14:  
  ![][image41]

### **Mathematical Equivalence and Verification**

To ensure the spatial allocation model remains mathematically consistent with the forecasted macroeconomic occupancy rate, the building-wide average simulated occupancy fraction at any time step ![][image18] must equal the uncoupled multiplicative formulation. This can be verified by summing the spatial occupancy schedules across all ![][image28] zones:  
![][image42]  
![][image43]  
This formulation ensures that the aggregated simulated load matches the macro-level forecast exactly, while the thermodynamic behavior of individual zones remains physically realistic.45 By avoiding the pitfall of multiplicative dilution, energy models can accurately simulate the thermal diversity of lodging properties, leading to more robust energy and peak-load projections up to the year 2030\.
